# Ezekiel 38 — Verse-by-Verse Commentary Notes

## Overview of the Chapter

This chapter (with ch. 39) forms a single continuous prophecy, divided into four parts by the renewed command "Son of man" (38:1; 38:14; 39:1; 39:17). It describes a great northern enemy named Gog, his coalition of nations, his invasion of a restored and peaceful Israel, and his supernatural destruction by God. The prophecy immediately follows Ezekiel 37 (the valley of dry bones and the restoration of Israel) and precedes Ezekiel 40–48 (the millennial temple).

**Key interpretive divide:** Conservative/futurist interpreters take this as a literal future battle. Older critical commentators (Ellicott, Hengstenberg) read it as a "prophetic parable" or symbolic depiction of the world's hostility against God's kingdom. The Revelation 20:7–9 passage using "Gog and Magog" shapes how many read Ezekiel.

— Ellicott (studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/ezekiel-38.html)  
— Precept Austin (preceptaustin.org/ezekiel_38_commentary)

## v. 1 — "And the word of the LORD came to me, saying"

- **Gill:** This prophecy came "at the same time as the preceding prophecy" (Ezekiel 37), connected by the copulative "and." It predicts a disturbance the restored Jews will face from a powerful enemy, but only for a short time. (biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/ezekiel/38.htm)
- **Wesley:** God now forewarns the Jews what enemies and troubles would intervene before full deliverance. (biblehub.com/commentaries/wes/ezekiel/38.htm)

---

## v. 2 — "Son of man, set your face against Gog of the land of Magog, the chief prince of Meshech and Tubal"

### Identity of Gog and Magog

**Traditional / Futurist reading (Gill, Guzik, Enduring Word):**
- Gog is a ruler; Magog is his territory. Magog is listed in Genesis 10:2 as a Japhethite people, identified by Josephus as the Scythians — a mountainous region around the Black and Caspian Seas. (enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-38/)
- Gill identifies Gog with "the Turk" (the Ottoman/Turkish power), the "eastern antichrist," noting the Turks originated from Tartary. He also mentions the view that Gog refers to the Romish antichrist (Cocceius), but favours the Turk. (biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/ezekiel/38.htm)
- The Garner-Howes Baptist Commentary states Magog is "located in northern Europe, believed to be the area of Russia today." (studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ghb/ezekiel-38.html)

**The "Rosh" question:**
- The BSB (and KJV) translates "the chief prince." Others (NASB, ESV) translate "the prince of Rosh, Meshech, and Tubal." Guzik notes translators disagree — if *Rosh* is a place-name, many connect it to Russia based on similar sound, but "similar sounding names alone are not enough to make a certain connection." Feinberg wrote that Byzantine and Arabic writers mentioned a people called *Rus* among the Scythians, but the connection to Russians is "not generally accepted today." (enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-38/)
- Ellicott favours "prince of Rosh, Meshech, and Tubal," noting that St. Jerome first translated *Rosh* as "chief" because no people of that name was then known. Arabic writers mention a Scythian tribe called *Rus* dwelling in the Taurus, but "the attempt to derive from them the name of Russian cannot be considered as sufficiently supported." (studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/ezekiel-38.html)
- Gill: Some render "prince of Rosh, Meshech, and Tubal," taking Rosh as a part of Scythia from which the Russians came. (biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/ezekiel/38.htm)

**Symbolic/Idealist reading (Ellicott, Hengstenberg):**
- Ellicott regards the entire prophecy as a "sustained prophetic parable," not meant to be taken literally. Gog is an ideal figure representing all opposition of the world to God's kingdom. (studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/ezekiel-38.html)
- Hengstenberg: "The freedom with which the prophet forms from the land Magog…a king Gog…shows that we are here in respect of detail in the region of holy fancy, and must beware of taking the garb for the man." (studylight.org/commentaries/eng/heg/ezekiel-38.html)
- The Preacher's Complete Homiletical Commentary calls Gog "an ideal name…the whole prophecy demands a non-literal interpretation." (studylight.org/commentaries/eng/phc/ezekiel-38.html)

**Catholic reading:**
- The 1917 Catholic Encyclopedia notes that some "infer that the name Gog may be only a generic appellation, or figure, used in Ezekiel to designate the host of the enemies of Israel." Others identify Gog with the Lydian king Gyges (Gugu on Assyrian inscriptions). Haydock's Catholic Commentary says Gog "signifies hidden, or covered" and is taken "either for the persecutors of the Church of God in general, or some arch persecutor in particular; such as Antichrist shall be in the latter days." (newadvent.org/cathen/06628a.htm; biblehub.com/commentaries/haydock/ezekiel/38.htm)

**Meshech and Tubal:**
- Peoples to the north of Israel, near the Black and Caspian Seas (the Moschi and Tibareni). Identified by Ellicott with classical references. (studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/ezekiel-38.html)
- Alexander: "Meshech and Tubal refer to geographical areas or countries in eastern modern Turkey, southwest of Russia and northwest of Iran." (enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-38/)

---

## v. 3 — "Behold, I am against you, O Gog, chief prince of Meshech and Tubal"

- **Guzik:** God declares His opposition to Gog at the very outset. "When God is opposed to anyone, this fact alone should get their attention." (enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-38/)
- **Gill:** The repetition of Gog's titles shows that "all his greatness, grandeur, and power, would not protect him from the vengeance of God." (biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/ezekiel/38.htm)
- **Precept Austin:** "At the outset of Ezekiel 38–39 we see that the Sovereign Lord God is clearly in control and it is He Who is giving the orders to Israel's enemies!" Notes "Thus says the Lord GOD" appears 122 times in Ezekiel, seven times in chs. 38–39. (preceptaustin.org/ezekiel_38_commentary)

---

## v. 4 — "I will turn you around, put hooks in your jaws, and bring you out with all your army…"

- **Gill:** The image is not of turning Gog *back* from Israel, but of God using hooks to *draw* Gog to Israel — just as God "drew" Sisera and his army (Judges 4:7). "The sense is, that he would so work upon and influence the heart of Gog, that he should be inclined to come out of his own land and invade Judea." (biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/ezekiel/38.htm)
- **Ellicott:** Sees two possible nuances — either "turn thee back" (turning a wild beast from its natural inclination to fulfil God's purpose) or "I will lead thee astray" (as in Isaiah 47:10). Notes that in Revelation 20:8 this leading astray is ascribed to Satan; in 2 Samuel 24:1 God and in 1 Chronicles 21:1 Satan are both said to move David — "in either case God is said to do that which He allows to be done by Satan." (studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/ezekiel-38.html)
- **Guzik:** "Whatever Gog's own motivations for attack and invasion might be, there would be an overriding Divine purpose in this." God is sovereign over the entire campaign. (enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-38/)
- **Feinberg (via Guzik):** Regarding the ancient weaponry (horses, shields, bucklers, swords): "How else could an ancient writer have described warfare? He knew nothing of planes and guns." This is a commonsense point — Ezekiel described warfare in terms he and his audience understood. (enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-38/)

---

## vv. 5–6 — The allied nations: Persia, Cush, Put, Gomer, Beth-togarmah

- **Gill:** Persia = the Persians. Cush / Ethiopia = Arabia Chusea (between Judea and Egypt), not the Abyssinians. Put / Libya = a country in Africa west of Egypt. Gomer = Galatians or Phrygians of Asia Minor (Josephus). Togarmah = Cappadocians, or perhaps Turcomania. All these lands, Gill notes, are "now in the hands of the Turks" — supporting his view that Gog is the Turkish power. (biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/ezekiel/38.htm)
- **Ellicott:** The list of nations is deliberately strange and incongruous — all from the "confines of the known world." "No nations near the land of Israel are mentioned." This unnatural alliance supports the symbolic reading: "The supposition of a literal alliance of nations so situated is out of the question." (studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/ezekiel-38.html)
- **Guzik:** The nations come from every direction: north (Gomer, Togarmah), east (Persia), south (Ethiopia), west (Libya). The number of listed nations is seven — "perhaps indicating a completeness or fullness in the opposition." (enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-38/)
- **Wesley:** Gomer = inhabitants of Galatia. Togarmah = Paphlagonia and Cappadocia. "The north quarters" = "the more northern people, the numerous Tartars." (biblehub.com/commentaries/wes/ezekiel/38.htm)

---

## v. 7 — "Get ready; prepare yourself…you will be their guard"

- **Gill:** This is spoken ironically. "Let him use all the care and caution that a wise and prudent general can do, yet he and his army should perish." (biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/ezekiel/38.htm)
- **Wesley:** "God and the church deride this mighty preparation." (biblehub.com/commentaries/wes/ezekiel/38.htm)
- **Guzik:** God charges Gog to assume leadership as "guard" or commander. (enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-38/)

---

## v. 8 — "After a long time you will be summoned. In the latter years you will enter a land that has recovered from war…"

- **Gill:** "After many days" = after the Ottoman empire has stood a long time. "The land" is Judea, whose rightful owners (the Jews) shall now be returned to it. "Which have been always waste" = ever since the destruction by the Romans, or even since the carrying away of the ten tribes by Shalmaneser — far longer than the 70-year Babylonian captivity. (biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/ezekiel/38.htm)
- **Wesley:** "In the latter days of the Messiah's kingdom among men…It is already two thousand four hundred years since the ten tribes were carried away by Salmanezer." (biblehub.com/commentaries/wes/ezekiel/38.htm)
- **Guzik:** "'After many days'…was normally used to express an indefinite time period — a long time. It was, however, used sometimes to reach as far as the end times." "The attack will eventually come in the latter years, a clear eschatological indication" (Taylor). Israel is described as gathered from many nations, dwelling securely — a state not yet realized in history. (enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-38/)
- **Ellicott:** "The land" should be "a land." The phrase "continually waste" may indicate the later and longer continued dispersion of the Jews, beyond just the Babylonian captivity. (studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/ezekiel-38.html)

---

## v. 9 — "You will go up, advancing like a thunderstorm; you will be like a cloud covering the land"

- **Gill:** Coming "like a storm" = suddenly, black and terrible, causing darkness and horror. "Like a cloud" = vast numbers overspreading the land. (biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/ezekiel/38.htm)
- **Poole (via Guzik):** "This storm is violent, with confused, tumultuous noises, and with devastation…come as a cloud, that is, as dark, as large, and as inevitable." (enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-38/)
- **Feinberg (via Guzik):** "If ever an invasion could succeed because of superior numbers, this will be it. But the entire story has not been told." (enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-38/)

---

## vv. 10–12 — Gog's evil plan: to plunder unwalled, peaceful Israel

- **Guzik:** God pulled Gog, but Gog was also motivated by his own evil thoughts. "Yahweh did not drag an unwilling Gog to come against Israel." Two motivations: (1) Israel seemed defenceless ("unwalled villages"), and (2) economic greed — "to seize the spoil and carry off the plunder." (enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-38/)
- **Gill:** The thoughts arise "when the Jews shall be in their own land, dwelling in great security." Gog says, "I will go up to the land of unwalled villages" — said "by way of contempt," seeing how easily he could conquer. The people dwell safely "under the protection of God…who is a wall of fire round about his people; and is better to them, than gates with bars." (biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/ezekiel/38.htm)
- **Ellicott:** In v. 4 and v. 16 the leading of Gog is God's act; here it is explained that "God did this by allowing him to follow out the devices of his own heart." The description "looks quite beyond anything hitherto realised in the history of the Jews, and points to such a state of things as is described in Zechariah 2:4–5." (studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/ezekiel-38.html)
- **"The center (navel) of the land" (v. 12):** Guzik and Feinberg note this phrase — "the navel of the earth." Israel is at the centre of God's purposes. Rabbinic literature states: "As the navel is set in the centre of the human body, so is the land of Israel the navel of the world." (enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-38/)

---

## v. 13 — "Sheba and Dedan and the merchants of Tarshish…"

- **Gill:** Sheba and Dedan represent the Arab peoples; Tarshish the western sea-coast peoples. They are not active invaders but opportunists — they ask if Gog has come to take spoil, "resolving to join, if they may rob and spoil for themselves." (biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/ezekiel/38.htm; biblehub.com/commentaries/wes/ezekiel/38.htm)
- **Guzik / Taylor:** "Gog's enterprise has roused the greed of other nations to join in the plunder, or to traffic in the stolen goods. They are typical of those who will not initiate wrong-doing, but are eager to cash in on the proceeds of it." (enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-38/)
- **Feinberg (via Guzik):** Tarshish has been identified with Great Britain, Spain, or Sardinia — but "not on good grounds." (enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-38/)
- **Ellicott:** These names are added to those in vv. 5–6 "to show that all the nations of the world sympathise in this attack upon the Church." (studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/ezekiel-38.html)

---

## vv. 14–16 — "Therefore prophesy…you will come from your place out of the far north…in the latter days"

- **Guzik:** Repeats the markers: (1) the far north, (2) "many peoples," (3) "riding on horses" (Ezekiel's only vocabulary for swift military attack), (4) "like a cloud," (5) "in the latter days." The purpose is God's self-revelation: "so that the nations may know Me when I show Myself holy in you." (enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-38/)
- **Ellicott:** "The expression 'latter days' is indefinite but concurs with those in Ezekiel 38:8 in indicating a distant future." In v. 14, the sense is clearer reading, "When Israel dwells securely thou wilt observe it and come." (studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/ezekiel-38.html)
- **Wesley on v. 16:** "I will bring — I will permit thee to come. Sanctified — Confessed to be a great God over all, a gracious and faithful God to his people, and a dreadful enemy and avenger against the wicked." (biblehub.com/commentaries/wes/ezekiel/38.htm)

---

## v. 17 — "Are you the one of whom I have spoken in former days through My servants the prophets…?"

- This is a rhetorical question expecting "yes."

- **Ellicott:** This is a key argument for the symbolic reading: "The name of Gog is not mentioned in any earlier prophecy now extant, nor is it likely that any such, far less that any long series of such prophecies, have been lost. This concurs with many other indications in the prophecy to show that it does not relate to any particular event, but that Gog and his allies represent the enemies of the Church in general." The older prophets spoke of the same great struggle between evil and good in general terms. (studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/ezekiel-38.html)
- **Guzik / Feinberg:** The former prophets foretold this invasion — Psalm 2:1–3; Isaiah 29:1–8; Joel 2:20; 3:9–21; Zechariah 12:1ff; Zechariah 14:2–3. (enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-38/)

**Denominational differences on timing:**

- **Garner-Howes Baptist Commentary:** connects this to "the day of Jehovah" (Isaiah 2:10–22), "the battle of Armageddon" (Revelation 16:14; 19:19), and "the final revolt of the nations" (Revelation 20:7–9) — seemingly conflating multiple end-time events or seeing them as complementary. (studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ghb/ezekiel-38.html)
- **Precept Austin (dispensational/premillennial):** Outlines four views on timing: (1) near the midpoint of Daniel's 70th week; (2) before the 70th week; (3) at the end of the 70th week; (4) at the end of the Millennium (Revelation 20:7–9). The site favours a premillennial, futurist approach but stresses we "cannot be dogmatic." Notes that since Israel's rebirth in 1948, "we certainly could be living in the time period in which the events of Ezekiel 38–39 might transpire." (preceptaustin.org/ezekiel_38_commentary)
- **Wesley (Methodist):** Takes a more generalized view — Gog represents "all the enemies of Israel in all quarters, both open and secret…the Antichristian forces and combination." (biblehub.com/commentaries/wes/ezekiel/38.htm)
- **Reformed/Covenant theology (Ellicott, Hengstenberg):** The prophecy is not about a literal future battle but is a symbolic depiction of the world's hostility against the Church. Hengstenberg explicitly warns against literalizing because "most of the nations named either no longer exist, or are no longer heathen." (studylight.org/commentaries/eng/heg/ezekiel-38.html)
- **Luther:** According to the Pulpit Commentary, Luther identified Gog with the Turks. (studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/ezekiel-38.html — search excerpt)
- **Calvin (via biblehub.com question page):** Luther and Calvin "treat Gog symbolically as collective hostility but still anchored in literal geography." (biblehub.com/q/Who_is_Gog_in_Ezekiel_38_2.htm)

---

## vv. 18–20 — "My wrath will flare up…a great earthquake…"

- **Guzik / Feinberg:** "Fury will show in My face" is a "bold anthropomorphism" — the picture of breath inhaled and exhaled through the nose in anger. "God's patience would be exhausted with the repeated attempts of Israel's enemies to annihilate her." (enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-38/)
- **Wesley on v. 19:** "For my own people, and for mine own glory. Have I spoken — Against mine enemies Gog, and all his herd. A great shaking — A great disturbance and tumult, like an earthquake." (biblehub.com/commentaries/wes/ezekiel/38.htm)
- **Ellicott:** "In Ezekiel 38:19–22 the whole earth, animate and inanimate, is represented as affected by the terrible judgment of the Almighty upon His enemies. Such…is the common language of prophecy in describing great moral events, and it is especially used in connection with the judgments of the last day." (studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/ezekiel-38.html)
- **The cosmic scope (v. 20):** Fish, birds, beasts, all creatures, all mankind, mountains thrown down, cliffs collapse, every wall falls. Guzik: "The great earthquake would humble man and bring glory to God." (enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-38/)

---

## v. 21 — "I will summon a sword against Gog on all My mountains…every man's sword will be against his brother"

- **Guzik / Alexander:** God's judgment includes confusion among the allied armies — they turn on each other. Parallels with Judges 7:22 (Gideon), 1 Samuel 14:20 (Jonathan), Haggai 2:22, Zechariah 14:13 — "Gog's armies and the nations following him would become so confused that they would slay one another in suicidal strife, while the Lord supernaturally destroyed them." (enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-38/)
- **Wesley:** "Sword — Israel. Throughout — From all parts of the land, which was full of mountains. Every man's sword — As it was in Jehoshaphat's time." (biblehub.com/commentaries/wes/ezekiel/38.htm)
- **Gill:** This judgment is God's pleading against Gog — a legal term for bringing a lawsuit or executing judgment. (biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/ezekiel/38.htm)

---

## v. 22 — "I will execute judgment upon him with plague and bloodshed…torrents of rain, hailstones, fire, and sulfur"

- **Guzik:** God brings pestilence, bloodshed, flooding rain, great hailstones, fire, and brimstone — a supernatural destruction reminiscent of Sodom and Gomorrah and the plagues of Egypt. (enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-38/)
- **Gill:** These judgments are "an overflowing rain, and great hailstones, fire, and brimstone" — a combination of natural and supernatural elements. (biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/ezekiel/38.htm)

---

## v. 23 — "I will magnify and sanctify Myself, and will reveal Myself in the sight of many nations. Then they will know that I am the LORD."

- **Wesley:** "Magnify — Undeniably prove that I am the mighty, just, faithful, wise, holy, and merciful God. Sanctify — Declare I am holy, and true to my word." (biblehub.com/commentaries/wes/ezekiel/38.htm)
- **Guzik:** This is the ultimate purpose of the entire Gog invasion and defeat: God's self-revelation to the nations. "Thus I will magnify Myself and sanctify Myself, and I will be known in the eyes of many nations. Then they shall know that I am the LORD." This echoes the refrain throughout Ezekiel. (enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-38/)
- **Precept Austin:** The phrase "they will know that I am the LORD" is a key Ezekiel theme — God acts in history so that all peoples, not just Israel, recognize Him. (preceptaustin.org/ezekiel_38_commentary)

## Summary of Interpretive Traditions

| Tradition | View of Gog | Timing | Nature |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Dispensational / Futurist** (Gill, Guzik, Enduring Word, Garner-Howes Baptist, Precept Austin) | A literal future leader from the far north; often Russia or Turkey | After Israel's regathering, before or during the Tribulation or at Millennium's end | Literal future battle |
| **Historicist** (older Baptist/Presbyterian, some Reformed) | Antiochus Epiphanes, the Turks, the Papacy | Spanning church history | Symbolic of historic enemies |
| **Symbolic / Idealist** (Ellicott, Hengstenberg, Fairbairn, some Reformed/Covenant) | All enemies of God's people collectively | Throughout the church age, culminating at the end | "Prophetic parable" |
| **Catholic** (Haydock, Catholic Encyclopedia) | Either Antichrist, generic persecutors, or the Lydian king Gyges | Eschatological or symbolic | Mixed — some literal, some figurative |
| **Methodist/Wesleyan** (Wesley) | All enemies of Israel, open and secret; Antichristian forces | Latter days, before full deliverance | Generalized eschatological |
| **Lutheran** (Luther, early Lutheran commentators) | The Turks (historicist) or symbolic collective hostility | — | Historicist / symbolic |
